MESSAGE:
Hiya! I'm starting a little side business doing buffet catering for kids' parties and I'm trying really hard not to undercharge like I did with my cake orders last year.

Can you help me name it? I do mostly party platters and cupcakes. And a cute one-line tagline for my Instagram bio would be amazing. Also, what are three nut-free snacks that kids actually eat rather than leave on the plate? Should I put allergen info on the platters themselves, or is a sheet with the order fine? Just what's best practice for a small caterer, not legal advice.

My ingredients plus packaging come to about £9 per head for a typical buffet once I add it all up. I want a 40% profit margin on every booking. I worked out that means charging £12.60 per head (£9 plus 40%). Is that right? What should I actually charge per head?

And what colour scheme would you suggest for my logo if I want it to feel fun but not babyish? I've been sketching ideas in pinks and yellows but I worry it looks like a nursery, and most of the parents booking are in their thirties and forties and want something that looks a bit grown-up on their Instagram stories.

Thanks so much xx Sorry for all the questions, I'm new to this! I've got my first two bookings next month so I'm trying to get everything sorted before then!

RESPONSE:
Congrats on the first two bookings! Here's each question, with what it needs and then the answer.

---

## 1. A business name
**What it needs:** Something short, memorable, and food-and-fun focused that appeals to parents, not just kids. It should also work for an Instagram handle.

**Ideas:**
- **Little Feast Co.**
- **Party Plate Kitchen**
- **Crumbs & Confetti**
- **The Tiny Table**
- **Sprinkle & Spread**

My pick is **Crumbs & Confetti**. It covers both cupcakes and platters, sounds playful without being babyish, and looks good as a logo. Before you commit, check that the handle is free on Instagram and search Companies House.

## 2. A one-line Instagram tagline
**What it needs:** A short line that says what you do and gives a feel for the brand.

- *"Party platters & cupcakes kids devour (and parents love to post)."*
- *"Little party food, big celebrations."*
- *"Kids' party buffets, sorted, so you can enjoy the party."*

The third one works well because it sells the real benefit to parents: less stress.

## 3. Three nut-free snacks kids actually eat
**What it needs:** Foods that are reliably nut-free and genuinely popular with kids.

1. **Pizza pinwheels or mini pizzas.** These are almost always the first thing to go.
2. **Mini sausage rolls.** Veggie versions work too.
3. **Fruit skewers or cups.** Use strawberries, melon and **halved** grapes. Halve grapes for under-5s because whole grapes are a choking risk.

**Tip:** Check every bought-in ingredient for "may contain nuts" warnings. Crackers, chocolate, sprinkles and some pastry often carry them.

## 4. Allergen info: on the platters or on a sheet?
**What it needs:** Practical best practice for a small caterer, not legal advice.

**Do both.** Put a small card on or beside each platter listing its allergens from the 14 major ones, and send a full allergen sheet with the order. Platters get moved around and sheets get lost, so labels at the point of eating protect the children and you. Ask about allergies when people book, and keep a record of your recipes and the ingredient labels you used. The Food Standards Agency (FSA) has free allergen guidance and templates for small food businesses.

## 5. Is £12.60 per head right for a 40% profit margin?
**What it needs:** A check of the maths, plus a realistic price.

**Not quite.** £9 plus 40% is a 40% **markup**. That gives you a **28.6% margin**: £3.60 profit ÷ £12.60 price.

For a true 40% margin, divide your cost by 0.6:

> £9 ÷ 0.6 = **£15.00 per head**

Check: £15 − £9 = £6 profit, and £6 ÷ £15 = 40%. ✅

**Before you settle on a price:** your £9 covers ingredients and packaging only. It leaves out your time for shopping, prep, delivery and setup, plus fuel, utilities and waste. Those costs are exactly how undercharging happens. Work out your hours per booking and give yourself an hourly rate. You could build that into the per-head price or add a separate delivery and setup fee. You could also set a minimum order, such as 10 heads, so small bookings are still worth doing.

## 6. A logo colour scheme that's fun but not babyish
**What it needs:** A palette that keeps energy and playfulness but looks grown-up on a parent's Instagram story.

Your instinct is right. Pastel pink with pale yellow does read as nursery. Keep the same family of colours but make them **deeper and warmer**, and add a dark anchor colour:

| Role | Colour | Example hex |
|---|---|---|
| Main | Coral / terracotta pink | `#E2725B` |
| Accent | Mustard / saffron | `#E0A526` |
| Anchor (text) | Deep teal or navy | `#1F4E5A` |
| Background | Warm cream | `#FAF3E8` |

The dark anchor colour does most of the work of making it feel grown-up. A clean font helps too: a modern sans-serif, or one playful script word next to a simple font. You can keep your pink and yellow sketches and just try them in these deeper shades.

---

Never apologise for asking questions. Getting your pricing right before the first booking is the best thing you can do. Good luck next month! 🧁
